q: My fabric supplier gave me its total factory emissions. How do I work out the share that belongs to my order?
title: Allocating a supplier's total emissions
short: Multiply the supplier's emissions by your share of its output. Use a physical basis, such as tonnes or metres of fabric, when its products are similar, and an economic basis, your share of its revenue, only when products differ a lot in value. Ask first whether the supplier can give a figure for your product line, which avoids allocation.
audience: Garment brands, buyers and procurement teams sourcing from shared mills

p: The GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard says to avoid allocation where possible. Ask the mill whether the line or process that makes your fabric is sub-metered, or whether it can give a footprint per kg for your quality. A figure for your product is always better than a share of a factory total.

ul: Physical (mass, metres, machine hours): best when the products go through similar processes. It follows how energy is actually used.

Economic (revenue): use when products share a process but differ greatly in value, or when no physical measure fits. It moves with prices, so a price change shifts emissions without any change on the factory floor.
Choose one basis, write it down, and use it every year for that supplier.
Which scopes: the mill's Scope 1 and 2 only, or also its own purchased yarn and chemicals. A cradle-to-gate figure needs both.
Which period and which sites, so it matches your purchase period.
Whether it covers non-fabric outputs, such as yarn sold to others or power exported, which should be taken out before you take your share.

sections.h: Record the basis with the number
p: Keep the supplier's document, the total, the denominator (total output or revenue), your purchase quantity and the method. An auditor will recompute the share, and a supplier figure with no stated basis is hard to defend.

example.title: Worked example: one fabric order, two allocation bases
lines: Mill emissions for the year: 8,000 t CO2e; mill output: 12,000 t of fabric
Mill revenue: Rs 300 crore; your purchases: Rs 24 crore, which is 8%
example.note: Your fabric is priced above the mill average, so economic allocation gives it more emissions. Use mass unless your fabric takes much more processing per tonne.

senseible: Senseible keeps the supplier's figure with its source document in the Scope 3 supplier evidence trail, so the allocation basis can be traced. It does not choose the allocation method or check the supplier's own total.
